summary: Live View becomes a video wall. An arrangement worth keeping is now a WALL: a name, a grid, and the cameras in the order you put them in, saved on the appliance instead of in the browser. That one change is most of the feature — the old arrangement lived in a cookie, so it existed only on the machine that built it, could not be handed to the operator on the next shift, could not be opened on a second monitor without being rebuilt by hand, and vanished when somebody cleared their browser. Walls are shared rather than personal, because a control room's walls are furniture and an administrator has to be able to fix the one everybody is looking at; one can be marked as the wall a screen opens with. Two numbers decide what a wall does while nobody is touching it. CYCLE advances through the pages every few seconds, so a station can watch more cameras than fit the grid. POP brings a camera onto the visible page when it raises an alert and holds it there, outlined, so it is obvious which camera the wall jumped for — and cycling pauses while it is showing, because a wall that rotates away two seconds later has done the opposite of raising an alarm. Paging by hand restarts the dwell, so a page you turned to is not whipped away a moment later. SECOND MONITOR opens the selected wall in its own window with no navigation and nothing else on screen, to be dragged onto another display and left there. It is a real browser window because a panel inside the app cannot be dragged to another screen. A wall that names a camera somebody has since deleted says so, rather than quietly rendering one tile fewer and letting an operator believe they are watching everything.
compatibility: Purely additive: one new auto-migrated table, no changes to any existing one, and the per-browser arrangement still works exactly as before for anyone who never saves a wall. Reading walls is part of the Live Views page a VIEWER already holds — a viewer who could not load the wall would see a blank grid — while creating, changing and removing them belongs to the same rung as moving a camera. No grantable level carries the DELETE verb, so removing a wall is a POST; that verb is kept for footage and records, and a wall is a list of camera ids that takes a minute to rebuild. Three unrelated defects were found and fixed while benching this. DELETING A CAMERA FAILED WITH A SERVER ERROR on any camera that had never produced an appearance descriptor, which — since appearance search is off by default — was most cameras on most installs: clearing descriptors that do not exist was being treated as a failure, and the failure aborted the camera-delete cascade by design. A camera delete that fails now also says why in the log, which it previously did not: server errors deliberately hide their detail from the caller, so the reason was lost entirely. And the landing page now carries the query string when it redirects into the app, so deep links survive it.
